and search
body:
Unit 2 · Intelligent Systems

School of Computer Science · Ciudad Real
Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha
Rubén Juárez Cádiz
notes: Unit 1 introduced the agent. Unit 2 focuses on an agent that uses a model to plan before acting. The cover is conceptual AI-generated artwork, not a graph to solve. The supplied 44-slide lecture is expanded with executable search traces, solved activities and precise algorithm assumptions.
ref: UCLM · Computer Science Degree

title: What you will be able to do
body:
FormulateTurn a task into states, actions, transitions, a goal and costs.
TraceFollow the frontier, selected node and repeated-state decisions.
CompareJustify completeness, cost optimality, time and memory.
ImplementConnect BFS, UCS, DFS, DLS and IDS to the Loopover lab.

The central question: which node should leave the frontier next?
notes: Suggested pacing: three 80-minute teaching blocks, adaptable to the timetable. Block one: formulation and search mechanics. Block two: uninformed algorithms and simulations. Block three: worked problems and laboratory implementation. Use the index to select sections rather than rush through every screen in one class. All interactive controls, notes and activities are in English. Simulations run offline.
sub: A framework for reasoning, tracing and building solvers
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: A goal does not specify a route
body:
“Reach the destination” tells us what counts as success.

Search finds an action sequence that can make it happen.
notes: Connect to Unit 1. A goal is a predicate on states, while a plan is a sequence of actions. Many plans may reach the same goal with different costs. The agent uses a model to explore possibilities without executing all of them in the real environment. Ask students to separate goal, plan and utility in a campus-delivery example.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Formulate, search and execute
body:
01UpdateInterpret the percept
02FormulateGoal and problem
03SearchFind a plan
04ExecuteTake an action
ModeWhat happens
Offline planningCompute a plan using a model before executing it.
Online searchInterleave action, observation and learning about an initially unknown environment.

A real agent may monitor execution and replan when its assumptions fail.
notes: The simplest classical problem-solving agent assumes a known initial state, deterministic transitions and a static planning setting. Under those assumptions it can execute a precomputed sequence. Monitoring and replanning extend that idealization. Online search is not a synonym for using the internet. It concerns interleaving computation with action and discovery.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Different uncertainty, different solutions
body:
Problem typeInformation availableForm of solution
Single-stateKnown current state and deterministic model.An action sequence.
ConformantInitial uncertainty with no observations during execution.A sequence that works for every possible state.
ContingentObservations or uncertain action outcomes matter.A conditional plan or policy.
ExplorationThe environment or transition structure is unknown.Act while acquiring a useful model.

This unit mainly studies deterministic, fully observable single-state problems.
notes: Uncertainty changes what a solution must represent. A fixed sequence need not work for every hidden state. A contingent solution branches on observations. In conformant planning, use a belief state representing all possibilities. These are scope distinctions; the algorithms developed next are not claimed to solve every uncertainty model.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: A precise search problem
body:
ComponentMeaning
Initial state s₀Where the search begins.
Actions A(s)Which actions are legal in a state.
Transition T(s,a)Which state results from a legal action.
Goal test G(s)Whether the objective has been reached.
Step cost c(s,a)The cost contributed by one action.

A solution is a legal action sequence. Its path cost is the sum of step costs.
notes: The source presents four components by combining actions and resulting states into a successor function. This presentation separates A and T, giving five entries without changing the model. The reachable state space is induced by the initial state and transitions. A goal can identify one state or many acceptable states. Costs must reflect the task rather than be inferred from the diagram’s visual geometry.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: An abstraction must preserve future choices
body:
Useful simplification

Route finding may represent a state by the current city.

Missing information

If fuel determines which roads are usable, city alone is insufficient.

A better state

(city, fuel) preserves the information needed for future actions.

Design test

Can identical encoded states have different legal futures?

Discard irrelevant detail while preserving actions, transitions, goals and costs.
notes: This is a state-sufficiency test. Search algorithms treat equal states as interchangeable for future planning. If the encoding omits remaining fuel or coin inventory, duplicate detection may incorrectly discard a necessary alternative. If time-dependent costs matter, the representation may also need time. History-dependent conditions must be represented or explicitly excluded by assumptions.
ref: Supplied material · Original state-design example

The three-edge path has cost 140+99+211=450. The four-edge path costs 140+80+97+101=418. In the original map Arad also connects to Timisoara and Zerind. For a BFS trace using alphabetical successor order, the first frontier is [Sibiu, Timisoara, Zerind], and expanding Sibiu produces [Timisoara, Zerind, Fagaras, Oradea, Rimnicu Vilcea] if the full textbook map is used. Always specify which graph is being traced.

title: A state graph and its search tree
body:
State-space graph

S → A → X
S → B → X

There is one state X, reached through two routes.

Search tree

S / A / X
S / B / X

There are two nodes containing X, each with its own path.

States describe configurations. Nodes describe paths that reach configurations.
notes: A state-space graph may be given explicitly or generated through a successor function. A search tree unfolds paths, so repeated states may appear many times. Do not equate the number of search nodes with the number of distinct states. If a cycle returns to S, tree search may produce infinitely many path nodes even when the graph is finite.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: A node stores more than a state
body:
FieldExamplePurpose
stateXConfiguration used by the problem model.
parentNode containing AReconstruct the selected path.
actionA_to_XRecord how the node was reached.
depth2Count actions from the root.
path cost g(n)7Accumulate step costs.

The same state may occur at different depths and path costs.
notes: The state representation should not include search bookkeeping such as a parent pointer merely to distinguish different paths. Node equality and state equality solve different problems. In Java, hash-based repeated-state control normally uses the immutable state representation. When a goal node is selected, follow parent links back to the root and reverse the actions.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Frontier, expansion and reached states
body:
FrontierCandidate nodes waiting to be selected.
SelectionRemove a candidate according to the strategy.
ExpansionGenerate legal successor states and child nodes.
Repeated-state controlTrack discovery, expansion or best known cost, depending on the algorithm.

Discovered, expanded and settled are different events.
notes: A discovered state has been generated. An expanded node has had successors considered. A settled state in uniform-cost search has been removed with its best cost under the algorithm’s assumptions. The source uses visited and explored loosely; in implementations these meanings must be explicit. We use goal testing after selection in the common simulator.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: A generic tree-search skeleton
body:
frontier ← [root(initial_state)]
while frontier is not empty:
    node ← remove_next(frontier)
    if goal(node.state):
        return reconstruct(node)
    for (action, state, cost) in successors(node.state):
        child ← Node(state, node, action,
                     node.depth + 1, node.g + cost)
        insert(frontier, child)
return FAILURE

The removal rule controls search order. Duplicate handling adds another design decision.
notes: This is explanatory pseudocode, not a finished Java implementation. It may revisit the same state arbitrarily many times. The root has depth and cost zero and no parent. A returned node encodes a path that must be reconstructed. The goal test is deliberately placed after frontier removal so later UCS discussion uses a consistent convention.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Repeated states require a policy
body:
PolicyWhat it preventsImportant consequence
Path cycle checkA state appearing twice on the current path.Uses little memory but allows repeats across branches.
Discovered-state setAdding a state already reached.Appropriate for ordinary equal-cost BFS.
Best-cost mapDiscarding a cheaper route to a known state.Needed for cost-based search such as UCS.
Depth-aware pruningDiscarding a state reached with more remaining depth.Relevant when implementing depth-limited graph search.

A boolean “visited” flag is not a substitute for every kind of repeated-state reasoning.
notes: BFS can mark a state on insertion because the first discovery has minimum depth under its assumptions. UCS may first discover an expensive path, so best-known costs must be improved. A depth-limited search can reach the same state with different remaining budgets; indiscriminate global pruning can lose a solution. The simple DLS demonstration later uses path-based cycle control.
ref: Supplied material · Algorithm-specific implementation clarification

title: BFS selects the shallowest candidate
body:
FIFO
queue

Insert new nodes at the back.
Remove the oldest node at the front.

Expansion order

All depth-0 nodes, then depth-1 nodes, then depth-2 nodes, and so on.

What it optimizes

The number of actions. This also minimizes cost when every action costs the same.

The ordering of successors resolves ties between nodes at the same depth.
notes: FIFO means first in, first out. A queue stores nodes, not just state labels, when paths must be reconstructed. Specify successor order before asking for a trace. On finite graphs, marking states when enqueued avoids unnecessary duplicate frontier entries. The first goal found has minimum depth. Unequal costs remove the general cost-optimality guarantee.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: One graph, three search strategies
body:
Selection order
Frontier · next candidate first

Directed edges carry positive costs. Successor order is alphabetical. Text labels identify selected and frontier states.
notes: Start with BFS, then reset and run UCS and DFS. The graph is an original example. Its edges are S→A:1, S→B:2, A→C:8, A→G:9, B→G:2 and C→D:1. BFS and DFS mark states when inserted. DFS pushes successors in reverse alphabetical order so A is examined before B. UCS uses best costs and stable insertion-order ties. The goal is tested after a non-stale node is selected. G is selected but not expanded. The simulator’s frontier shows the next selection first. All numerical traces elsewhere refer to this exact graph.
ref: Original graph and executable simulation

title: BFS: the queue explains the result
body:
SelectedQueue afterwardsWhat happened
SA(1), B(2)Discover the two depth-1 nodes.
AB(2), C(9), G(10)Discover C and G at depth 2.
BC(9), G(10)G is already discovered.
CG(10), D(10)Discover D at depth 3.
GStopReturn S → A → G, cost 10.

Numbers in parentheses are path costs, not queue priorities. BFS prioritizes depth.
notes: At B, another path to G has cost 4, but standard BFS does not improve paths by monetary or distance cost. Its promise is minimum depth. Both S-A-G and S-B-G contain two actions. With the stated successor order, S-A-G is the first goal path. This is not a bug in BFS; it illustrates a mismatch between a cost objective and a depth-based strategy.
ref: Calculated trace of the shared simulation

title: BFS guarantees and memory cost
body:
QuestionAnswer with assumptions
Complete?Yes for finite branching when a solution exists at finite depth.
Cost-optimal?Yes when step costs are equal and positive.
Main resource riskAn exponentially large frontier.
Finite explicit graphStandard adjacency-list BFS takes O(V + E) time and O(V) space.

Tree-size bounds and explicit-graph bounds describe different representations.
notes: For an implicit search tree, complexity is expressed using branching and solution depth. With our goal test on removal, nodes one level below depth d may already have been generated, yielding a conservative O(b^(d+1)) time and memory bound. A generation-time BFS goal test can stop earlier. A finite explored graph may eventually return failure; completeness does not mean failure can be detected in finite time for every infinite unsolvable graph.
ref: Supplied material · Complexity conventions clarified

title: How quickly does a tree grow?
body:
A full b-ary tree, no repeated states and all levels counted.

Nodes at depth d · bᵈ
Nodes through depth d · Σᵢ₌₀ᵈ bⁱ
At an assumed 128 bytes per retained node

The memory estimate is illustrative. Real nodes and data structures have additional overhead.
notes: Vary depth before branching. This is an exact count for the stated full-tree model, not a measurement of a real Java implementation. The bytes-per-node assumption is explicitly hypothetical. The displayed memory is total full-tree nodes multiplied by 128 bytes, in binary units. It is not claimed that every BFS implementation retains every generated node. Duplicate removal and earlier goal tests can reduce work.
ref: Original counting model and interactive calculator

title: UCS selects the lowest path cost
body:
Priority
queue
priority(n) = g(n)

Different objective

A deeper path may still be cheaper.

Different duplicate rule

If a cheaper route reaches a known state, update its best cost and candidate path.

The first discovered route to a state need not be its cheapest route.
notes: Uniform-cost search is a goal-directed version of Dijkstra-style shortest-path exploration with suitable costs. A priority queue may support decrease-key, or it may contain a new entry while the old one is later skipped as stale. The simulator uses the latter approach. Equal positive step costs make cost order agree with depth order, apart from tie-breaking.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Best costs and stale entries
body:
best[start] ← 0; push(root, priority=0)
while frontier is not empty:
    n ← pop_min_g()
    if n.g != best[n.state]: continue
    if goal(n.state): return reconstruct(n)
    for (a, s, cost) in successors(n.state):
        new_g ← n.g + cost
        if new_g < best.get(s, infinity):
            best[s] ← new_g
            push(Node(s, n, a, new_g), priority=new_g)
return FAILURE

The goal test follows stale-entry rejection and minimum-cost selection.
notes: This is abbreviated pseudocode. A real node also records depth and any deterministic tie-break identifier. best is keyed by immutable state. With nonnegative edge costs, a non-stale node removed at minimum g has settled optimal cost. With strictly positive lower-bounded costs and finite branching, UCS is also complete for finite-cost solutions in the usual infinite-tree setting. Do not copy a discovered-state boolean from BFS into this algorithm.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: UCS improves an expensive discovery
body:
SelectedActive candidates, lowest g firstEffect
S(0)A(1), B(2)Initialize alternative routes.
A(1)B(2), C(9), G(10)An expensive goal path is discovered.
B(2)G(4), C(9)Improve G from 10 to 4.
G(4)StopReturn S → B → G.

G(10) may remain physically in the heap, but it is stale and must not be accepted.
notes: The shared simulation displays all queued entries and labels stale ones. The compact table shows active entries only. When B is expanded, g(B)+c(B,G)=2+2=4 beats 10. G(4) is removed before C(9), giving the cheapest route. The old G(10) entry does not harm correctness if it is rejected when selected.
ref: Calculated trace of the shared simulation

title: Discovering a goal is not enough
body:
A discovers G with cost 10.
B later offers G with cost 4.

Stopping on generation

May accept the expensive route before cheaper alternatives are considered.

Stopping on selection

Accepts a non-stale goal removed at minimum g under UCS assumptions.

The position of one goal test can change the correctness of an algorithm.
notes: This is the same graph rather than an unrelated counterexample. Generate successors of A before expanding B and ask students whether the task is solved optimally yet. It is not. Early generation-time termination is valid for certain BFS implementations with equal action costs, but that rule cannot be transferred blindly to UCS.
ref: Counterexample from the shared simulation

title: UCS: separate optimality and completeness
body:
SettingWhat can be guaranteed
Finite reachable graph, nonnegative costsCorrect graph UCS terminates and returns a cheapest reachable goal.
Infinite setting, finite branching, cost ≥ ε > 0A finite-cost solution will be reached.
Infinite zero-cost regionSearch may never reach a positive-cost goal.
Negative edgesThe usual settle-on-removal argument fails.

A zero lower bound and a positive lower bound are not interchangeable.
notes: On a finite graph, strict best-cost improvement and repeated-state control handle zero-cost cycles without repeatedly improving the same state. In an infinite setting, infinitely many zero-cost states can starve a positive-cost goal. A positive lower bound ε limits how many actions fit within a finite cost budget. Negative-edge problems require a different algorithm and assumptions. Keep these distinctions when interpreting summary tables.
ref: Supplied material · AIMA / CS188 assumptions checked

title: DFS follows one branch first
body:
LIFO
stack

Insert new nodes on top.
Remove the most recently inserted node.

In the shared graph

Selection order:
S, A, C, D, G

Returned path

S → A → G, with cost 10.

The selected-node order is not the solution path.
notes: The shared DFS implementation marks states on insertion and pushes successors in reverse alphabetical order. G is discovered from A before the dead-end C-D branch is explored. When D has no successors, G is selected. Parent links reconstruct S-A-G, not the entire selection trace. This is a useful opportunity to distinguish traversal order from a returned plan.
ref: Supplied material · Calculated simulator trace

title: Low-memory claims need an implementation
body:
DFS variantMemory behaviourCompleteness caveat
Tree / path-based DFSO(bm) with stored siblings, or O(m) with lazy successor iteration.Can descend forever without reaching a goal.
Finite graph DFS with a global visited setStores up to O(V) visited states as well as the traversal state.Complete over a finite reachable graph with correct duplicate handling.
Either versionNo general minimum-depth or minimum-cost guarantee.Successor ordering can strongly affect the first result.

Adding a global visited set changes the memory model.
notes: The source correctly emphasizes DFS memory savings but a blanket O(bm) statement must refer to a tree or path-based implementation. The simulator stores a global discovered set and therefore also consumes memory proportional to visited states. In infinite acyclic spaces even cycle detection cannot prevent endless descent. A depth bound addresses that particular risk, but may exclude the goal.
ref: Supplied material · Implementation-dependent qualification

title: Depth-limited search has three outcomes
body:
SOLUTIONA goal was found within the limit.
CUTOFFA potentially useful branch was stopped by the limit.
FAILUREAll available branches were exhausted without finding a goal or being cut off.

CUTOFF means “the limit prevented a conclusion”, not “there is no solution”.
notes: Let the depth limit be ℓ. DLS explores depth-first but stops beyond ℓ. If a goal lies deeper, the search may return cutoff. Distinguish that result from genuine failure, because IDS must continue after cutoff. The demonstration recognizes terminal dead ends as failure even when they occur at the depth limit. This is a slightly more informative version of the common textbook rule that returns cutoff immediately at the bound.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: A depth limit you can change
body:
Edges: S→A, S→B, A→C, B→D, C→G.
G is at depth 3. D is a terminal dead end.

Result
Visited nodes in this run

Increasing the limit can change CUTOFF into SOLUTION.
notes: Run limits zero through three. With alphabetical traversal: ℓ=0 visits S and cuts off; ℓ=1 visits S,A,B and cuts off; ℓ=2 visits S,A,C,B,D and cuts off because C could continue; ℓ=3 visits S,A,C,G and finds the solution. At ℓ=4 the same goal is found before the larger bound. These are counts for this specific tree, not general complexity formulas.
ref: Original DLS demonstration

title: IDS increases the limit systematically
body:
for limit = 0, 1, 2, ...:
    result ← depth_limited_search(initial_state, limit)
    if result is SOLUTION: return result
    if result is FAILURE: return FAILURE
    # CUTOFF: try the next limit
01ℓ = 0Root only
02ℓ = 1One action
03ℓ = 2Two actions
04ℓ = 3Three actions

With finite branching, IDS finds a finite-depth solution without keeping a BFS-sized frontier.
notes: Each iteration performs a fresh depth-limited traversal. Path-based cycle checking avoids loops within the current path. Do not carry a naive global visited set across iterations, since states pruned at a small limit must be revisited with a larger remaining budget. IDS finds a shallowest goal, hence minimum cost when step costs are equal and positive. Unequal costs remove that cost guarantee.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Repeated work can still be affordable
body:
Full tree through depth 5Single traversal countIDS total count
b = 263120
b = 10111,111123,456

Why the overhead is limited

In a branching tree, most nodes occur near the deepest level.

What the counts assume

Every level is fully explored. No early goal stop and no duplicate pruning.

For b > 1, the overhead ratio approaches b / (b − 1) as depth grows.
notes: The single traversal count is Σ b^i for i from 0 to d. IDS counts each depth-i node d+1−i times, giving Σ(d+1−i)b^i. At b=2,d=5 the counts are 63 and 120; at b=10,d=5 they are 111111 and 123456. These are model counts, not measured runtimes. With b=1, IDS can have quadratic rather than linear work in depth, so the branching assumption matters.
ref: Supplied idea · Original calculated examples

title: Completeness and cost optimality
body:
StrategyComplete?Cost-optimal?Main trade-off
BFSYes¹With equal positive costsLarge frontier.
UCSYes²With nonnegative costs³Cost-ordered frontier and best-cost storage.
DFSNot in general; yes on finite spaces with safe cycle controlNoTraversal depth versus visited-state memory.
DLSOnly when the limit is sufficient⁴No in generalA wrong limit cuts off solutions.
IDSYes¹With equal positive costsRepeated shallow work, small path memory.

¹ Finite branching and finite-depth solution. ² Positive lower-bounded costs for the usual infinite-space result. ³ Correct best-cost handling and a goal removed from the queue. ⁴ Finite search to the bound with safe cycle handling.
notes: This table deliberately preserves conditions instead of using unqualified yes/no answers. For a finite graph, UCS also handles zero costs as discussed earlier. For DLS, an adequate limit makes a finite-depth solution discoverable, but DFS order may still return a nonminimal path. Cost optimality means minimum total step cost, not merely fewest actions.
ref: Supplied comparison · Conditions made explicit

title: Notation that keeps the claims precise
body:
SymbolMeaning
bMaximum branching factor.
dDepth of the shallowest goal, not necessarily the cheapest goal.
mMaximum depth considered by the search tree or traversal.
ℓChosen depth limit.
C*Cost of an optimal solution.
εA positive lower bound on step costs, when assumed.

Do not replace d with “depth of the least-cost solution” when costs differ.
notes: The source combines shallowest and least-cost depth in one label. They agree only under appropriate equal-cost assumptions. In a cyclic finite graph, the unrestricted search tree may have infinite depth even though the state count is finite. That is why m is a search-tree or traversal quantity rather than simply the number of states.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Tree-based worst-case growth
body:
StrategyTime boundSpace bound
BFS, goal tested on removalO(b^(d+1))O(b^(d+1))
UCS, cost ≥ ε > 0O(b^(1 + ⌊C*/ε⌋))O(b^(1 + ⌊C*/ε⌋))
DFS, finite maximum depth mO(b^m)O(bm)
DLS with limit ℓO(b^ℓ)O(bℓ)
IDS, b > 1O(b^d)O(bd)

Conventions: finite branching b > 1, implicit trees, stored siblings for DFS-style space. A global reached map adds memory. Explicit finite-graph bounds use V and E instead.
notes: These are standard conservative tree-search bounds with the conventions stated on the slide. They describe asymptotic growth, not exact node counts. Optimized BFS with generation-time goal testing is often summarized with O(b^d). There is no contradiction once the convention is specified. UCS explores nodes affordable within the optimal-cost budget and may generate one extra layer. The table does not assume a heuristic.
ref: Supplied material · Standard search bounds with explicit conventions

title: Choosing a strategy from the task
body:
Equal costs and ample memoryBFS is a straightforward way to obtain a shortest action sequence.
Different nonnegative costsUCS handles the actual accumulated cost.
A shallow solution and tight memoryPath-based IDS is often a useful starting point.
A justified maximum depthDLS makes the bound explicit.
Traversal without an optimality requirementDFS may be appropriate if its termination conditions are controlled.

Choose the objective and constraints before choosing the data structure.
notes: These are conditional design suggestions, not universal rankings. If memory is strict, measure the visited structure as well as the frontier. A known finite graph may justify global DFS. If actions have different costs, IDS optimizes depth rather than cost. Later informed-search methods can use domain knowledge but still depend on a correct problem model.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: The 8-puzzle as a state space
body:
Supplied initial board

7245□6831

Goal board

12345678□

State: tile arrangement. Actions: legal blank moves. Cost: one per move.
notes: The blank is a position, not an extra numbered tile. Generate only moves within the 3×3 board. There are 9! arrangements, but a fixed goal is reachable from only one parity class, with 9!/2 = 181440 states. For the supplied starting sequence, ignoring the blank gives 16 inversions, an even number, so it is solvable relative to the shown goal on this odd-width board. Do not transfer this parity rule unchanged to even-width puzzles.
ref: Supplied board · Calculated parity check

title: The vacuum world: modelling the full state
body:
s = (location, dirtA, dirtB)
2 × 2 × 2 = 8 states

Goal: both dirt flags are false.

ActionsLeft, right, suck and optionally wait.
TransitionUpdate the location or current dirt flag.
Cost conventionOne per non-wait action. Waiting can be omitted from the search.

This search model uses a known full state. Unit 1’s local sensor alone does not provide it.
notes: The distinction from the partially observable agent in Unit 1 is intentional. A single-state search assumes a known initial configuration and a deterministic model. With only a local observation, one would instead need a belief-state formulation or additional information. A no-op self-loop creates no progress and can usually be excluded when planning solely to reach a clean state. If it has zero cost, duplicate handling is important.
ref: Adapted from the supplied Unit 2 material

title: Limited-inventory coin change

State = ((n50, n10, n5, n1), remaining). Goal: remaining = 0. Cost: one per coin.

Inventory is part of the state because it constrains future choices. The four quantities together sum to 99 cents. Taking coins in different orders may reach the same state, which motivates duplicate detection.

title: Why greedy coin choice is a separate claim
body:
A different coin system

Values {4, 3, 1}, unlimited supply.
Target: 6.

Largest-first choice

4 + 1 + 1 uses three coins.

A better solution

3 + 3 uses two coins.

What follows

A plausible local rule is not automatically a proof of global optimality.

This counterexample changes the coin system. It is not a claim about the supplied inventory.
notes: The exercise separates modelling from algorithm justification. Students may recognize canonical coin systems where a greedy rule is optimal, but that result depends on denomination and inventory conditions. BFS obtains a minimum-coin solution for this small equal-cost state-space model without assuming a greedy-choice property.
ref: Original counterexample with explicitly different denominations

title: River crossing: compact state and safety
body:
s = (Mₗ, Cₗ, boat)

Initial: (3, 3, L)
Goal: (0, 0, R)

Right-bank counts follow from:
Mᵣ = 3 − Mₗ, Cᵣ = 3 − Cₗ.

Boat capacity

One or two passengers per crossing.

Safety on each bank

If missionaries are present, they cannot be outnumbered.

M = 0 or M ≥ C

The zero-missionary case matters: a bank containing only cannibals is legal.
notes: This is the classic missionaries-and-cannibals puzzle retained from the supplied material. M and C identify the two participant types in the textbook story. Legal states satisfy bounds from zero to three and the safety condition on both banks. Boat location is necessary because it controls available departures. All crossings cost one. The simplified state avoids storing redundant right-bank counts.

title: A small implementation contract
body:
ImmutabilityGenerating a child must not alter its parent’s state.
EqualityEquivalent configurations must compare equal and have consistent hashes.
Cost propagationchild.g = parent.g + successor.cost.
Path reconstructionFollow parent pointers, collect actions and reverse the result.
Deterministic tiesSpecify successor order and tie-breaking for reproducible traces.

A search algorithm cannot compensate for an incorrect transition function.
notes: For array-backed Java states, beware of shared mutable references. If hash keys change after insertion, set and map lookup becomes unreliable. For priority queues, use a stable secondary key when reproducible teaching traces matter. Keep generated-node, expanded-node and frontier-size counters separately defined. These implementation principles do not prescribe a particular library or project structure.
ref: Original implementation guidance tied to the supplied lab

title: Tests that check the model, not just the output
body:
CheckWhat a failure reveals
Known transition 02+Wrong operation order, direction or index.

Parent unchangedAliasing or mutable-state leakage.
Goal inputIncorrect empty-plan handling.
Different-cost graphA UCS best-cost or goal-test error.

A visually plausible route is not sufficient evidence that the solver is correct.
notes: These are proposed checks for students. Add illegal encodings and out-of-range action labels when testing parsing. Use independent small graphs with known optimal costs to separate search bugs from Loopover transition bugs. With random test generation, preserve the seed. Memory and time caps should be explicit, and reaching a cap should not be reported as a proof of no solution.

Use alphabetical successor order, a goal test on removal and the duplicate policies described with the simulation. For IDS, assume path-based DLS with alphabetical children. title: Six checks before implementing
body:
01

State or node: which has a parent?

The node. State equality describes the configuration, not its path.
02

When does BFS minimize cost?

Equal positive step costs turn minimum depth into minimum cost.
03

When can UCS accept a goal?

When a non-stale goal is selected with the lowest path cost.
04

Why improve a known state in UCS?

Its first discovered path may be more expensive.
05

What does CUTOFF mean?

The depth bound stopped a branch that could continue.
06

What does IDS repeat?

Fresh depth-limited searches with progressively larger limits.
notes: Use this as retrieval practice rather than showing all answers immediately. Follow up each answer with a counterexample: two paths to one state, unequal road distances, an expensive first goal, or a deeper reachable goal. In the PDF, all explanations are visible for self-study.
ref: Original learning check

Good search begins with a correct abstraction and ends with a justified claim.
notes: Distinguish failure from timeout, memory exhaustion and depth cutoff. A solver that cannot continue has not necessarily proved unsolvability. Also separate an algorithm’s theoretical guarantee from a single successful test. Tie each guarantee to the implementation assumptions used throughout the unit.

title: What if the agent knew where to look?
body:
Uninformed search orders candidates using depth or accumulated cost.

Unit 3 adds a heuristic

h(n)

An estimate of the remaining cost.

A question to carry forward

When does that estimate speed up search without losing the guarantee we need?

The state model, legal transitions, path cost and goal test remain essential.
notes: Do not describe uninformed search as literally having no information. It uses the problem definition, and UCS uses path costs. Informed search adds domain guidance, typically a heuristic estimate. This closes the unit without teaching A* prematurely. Ask students what a useful estimate might be for route finding or a tile puzzle.
